D.treatment: assessment tools at the two highest Miller levels
D.comparison: assessment tools at the two lower Miller levels

O.outcome_detail: number of tools available by Miller competency level

cells.quote: Twenty of these tools assessed the two highest Miller levels (‘shows how’ and ‘does’) and four tools were directed at multiple levels.
cells.note: The review reports descriptive tool counts, not an intervention effect.

D.comparison: tools assessing optimising human and environmental factors

O.outcome_detail: coverage of Canadian safety competency domains

cells.quote: Referring back to the six aforementioned domains of the Canadian Safety Competencies Framework, 25 of our tools (74%) assessed the ‘managing safety risks’ competencies, and 24 tools (71%) measured the ‘working in teams for patient safety’ competencies. Approximately half of the tools (16 tools, 47%) assessed the ‘communicating effectively for patient safety’ competencies, and 12 tools (35%) evaluated the ‘contributing to a culture of patient safety’ competencies. Six tools (18%) assessed the ‘recognizing, responding to, and disclosing adverse events’ competencies, while only four tools (12%) measured the ‘optimizing human and environmental factors’ competencies.
cells.note: The review reports domain-coverage counts rather than comparative learning outcomes.

O.outcome_detail: number of tools with reported reliability or validity evidence

cells.quote: The issue of content validity was raised in the descriptions of 14 tools (41%). According to the response process, rater-training was described for nine tools (26%), usually only once and briefly. The matter of internal structure was mentioned for 22 tools (65%).
cells.note: These are counts of reported validity evidence, not estimates of comparative assessment quality.
